claim: Insects find food and mates by navigating odorant plumes that can be highly intermittent, with intensities and durations that vary rapidly over orders of magnitude.
source: Insects find food and mates by navigating odorant plumes that can be highly intermittent, with intensities and durations that vary rapidly over orders of magnitude.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on insect navigation and odor plume structure.

claim: ORNs adapt to stimulus mean and variance.
source: By stimulating Drosophila ORNs in vivo with naturalistic and Gaussian stimuli, we show that ORNs adapt to stimulus mean and variance, and that adaptation and saturation contribute to naturalistic sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ORN responses to stimuli with varying means and variances.

claim: Mean-dependent gain control followed the Weber-Fechner relation.
source: Mean-dependent gain control followed the Weber-Fechner relation and occurred primarily at odor transduction, while variance-dependent gain control occurred at both transduction and spiking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements showing gain scaling inversely with mean stimulus intensity.

claim: Mean-dependent gain control occurred primarily at odor transduction.
source: Mean-dependent gain control followed the Weber-Fechner relation and occurred primarily at odor transduction, while variance-dependent gain control occurred at both transduction and spiking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in LFP responses but not firing machinery responses to mean stimulus changes.

claim: Variance-dependent gain control occurred at both transduction and spiking.
source: Mean-dependent gain control followed the Weber-Fechner relation and occurred primarily at odor transduction, while variance-dependent gain control occurred at both transduction and spiking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in both LFP and firing rate responses to variance changes.

claim: Transduction and spike generation possessed complementary kinetic properties that preserved the timing of odorant encounters in ORN spiking, regardless of intensity.
source: Transduction and spike generation possessed complementary kinetic properties, that together preserved the timing of odorant encounters in ORN spiking, regardless of intensity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that while LFP kinetics slow down with increasing stimulus, firing rate kinetics remain invariant.

claim: Turbulent airflows shape odor plumes into intermittent whiffs separated by stochastic durations of background air.
source: Instead, turbulent airflows shape odor plumes into intermittent whiffs separated by stochastic durations of background air (blanks).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on odor plume structure.

claim: The intensity of whiffs is typically distributed according to a power law.
source: First, the intensity of whiffs is typically distributed according to a power law (Murlis et al., 1992), with intense whiffs interleaved unpredictably with weak ones (Riffell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing odor plume statistics.

claim: Whiff durations and blank durations are distributed as a power law over a wide range of time scales.
source: Second, whiff durations and blank durations are also distributed as a power law over a wide range of time scales (Celani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work on odor plume statistics.

claim: A single odorant can be detected by multiple receptor types with different sensitivities.
source: A single odorant can be detected by multiple receptor types, with different sensitivities(Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing odorant receptor sensitivities.

claim: Static compressive nonlinearities at both ORNs and PNs selectively amplify weak signals and suppress responses to large signals.
source: Static compressive nonlinearities at both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and their post-synaptic targets, the projection neurons (PNs), selectively amplify weak signals and suppress responses to large signals (Bhandawat et al., 2007; de Bruyne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing ORN and PN response properties.

claim: Glomerular mechanisms implement a type of divisive gain control that maintains PN sensitivity within the range of changing ORN responses.
source: Glomerular mechanisms implement a type of divisive gain control that maintains PN sensitivity within the range of changing ORN responses (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2010; Olsen and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on antennal lobe processing.

claim: Transduction currents in response to odor pulses scale inversely with the intensity of the background signal, consistent with the Weber-Fechner Law.
source: Finally, transduction currents in response to odor pulses scale inversely with the intensity of the background signal, consistent with the Weber-Fechner Law (Cafaro, 2016; Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on ORN adaptation.

claim: Whether ORN firing follows Weber-Fechner scaling is unclear.
source: However, whether ORN firing follows a similar scaling is unclear (Cafaro, 2016; Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work showing conflicting or incomplete results.

claim: Transduction can be initiated within milliseconds of odor reaching the antenna.
source: Transduction can be initiated within milliseconds of odor reaching the antenna (Szyszka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work measuring transduction speed.

claim: ORN spike generation emphasizes changes in transduction currents.
source: The speed of the response is enhanced by ORN spike generation, which emphasizes changes in transduction currents (Nagel and Wilson, 2011), and by PNs (Kim et al., 2015), which maintain fast information transmission from ORNs to PNs (Jeanne and Wilson, 2015; Nagel et al., 2015; Raccuglia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing ORN and PN response properties.

claim: Adaptation to high intensity stimuli slows down transduction.
source: In contrast, adaptation to high intensity stimuli slows down transduction (Cao et al., 2016; Kaissling et al., 1987; Nagel and Wilson, 2011), a property that might make it difficult to reliably encode the timing of odor encounters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on ORN adaptation kinetics.

claim: ab2A and ab3A ORNs responded to whiffs with transient decreases in the local field potential (LFP) and corresponding increases in the firing rate.
source: ab2A and ab3A ORNs responded to whiffs with transient decreases in the local field potential (LFP) and corresponding increases in the firing rate (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Responses to faint whiffs were amplified more than those to intense whiffs.
source: Even though individual whiff intensities were broadly distributed (First line in Figure 1a) ORN responses to these whiffs were more even, so that responses to faint whiffs were amplified more than those to intense whiffs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Changes in gain do not arise solely from a static output nonlinearity.
source: Variations in the gain (ΔR/ΔS) clearly do not arise solely from a static output nonlinearity, such as one associated with a linear-nonlinear transformation, since plotting neuron response against the projected stimulus (Figure 1c–d) does not yield a single transformative function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-d and logical inference from the data.

claim: A clear sigmoidal dependency is visible in the plot of LFP responses against whiff intensity, consistent with a front-end nonlinearity arising from receptor-odorant binding.
source: A clear sigmoidal dependency is visible in the plot of LFP responses against whiff intensity, consistent with a front-end nonlinearity arising from receptor-odorant binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and inference based on known receptor-ligand binding properties.

claim: Responses to whiffs with similar intensities varied significantly, deviating from a single sigmoidal dose-response curve.
source: However, in both the LFP and firing rates, responses to whiffs with similar intensities varied significantly, deviating from a single sigmoidal dose-response curve (Figure 1e–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e-f.

claim: The amplitude of LFP and firing rate responses elicited by whiffs varied inversely with the amplitude of the preceding stimulus.
source: The amplitude of LFP and firing rate responses elicited by these whiffs varied inversely with the amplitude of the preceding stimulus: whiffs that occurred in isolation (purple) elicited the largest responses, while whiffs that followed earlier, large whiffs (blue, red) elicited the smallest responses, suggesting that ORN responses can be modulated by stimulus history.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: Deviations in LFP response to each whiff decreased with mean stimulus in the preceding 300 ms.
source: Deviations in LFP response to each whiff decreased with mean stimulus in the preceding 300 ms (Figure 2c, ρ=−0.39, p=0.01, Spearman test), and were uncorrelated with the amplitude of the whiff that elicited them (Figure 2c, inset, p=0.9, Spearman test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When response deviations were negative, the amplitude of the preceding whiffs tended to be larger, and the time since the previous whiff tended to be shorter.
source: When response deviations were negative (smaller than median responses, blue dots), the amplitude of the preceding whiffs tended to be larger, and the time since the previous whiff tended to be shorter.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e-f.

claim: ORN gain in each trial varied with the mean stimulus in that trial as an approximate power law with exponent –1.
source: ORN gain in each trial varied with the mean stimulus in that trial as an approximate power law with exponent –1 (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: This exponent is consistent with the Weber-Fechner Law.
source: This exponent is consistent with the Weber-Fechner Law, which postulates that the just noticeable difference between two stimuli is inversely proportional to the stimulus magnitude (Stevens, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work defining the Weber-Fechner Law and inference from the measured exponent.

claim: Rescaling the projected stimulus by the gain predicted by Weber's Law collapsed all input-output curves onto a single curve.
source: Rescaling the projected stimulus by the gain predicted by Weber's Law collapsed all input-output curves onto a single curve (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In all five cases tested, the neurons decreased gain with increasing odorant concentration, and obeyed a roughly inverse scaling.
source: In all five cases, the neurons decreased gain with increasing odorant concentration, and obeyed a roughly inverse scaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f.

claim: ORN firing rate variance did not vary as much as the stimulus variance between epochs of high and low stimulus variances.
source: Interestingly, ORN firing rate variance did not vary as much as the stimulus variance between epochs of high and low stimulus variances, suggesting that ORNs actively changed their gain to compensate for such input differences (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c-d and inference from the data.

claim: ORN input-output curves during high variance epochs were shallower than during low variance epochs.
source: ORN input-output curves during high variance epochs (red) were shallower than during low variance (blue) epochs (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Trial-wise ORN gain decreased with the variance of the stimulus.
source: Trial-wise ORN gain decreased with the variance of the stimulus (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: On a trial-by-trial basis, ORN gain was correlated with the c.d.f slope (r2 = 0.7).
source: On a trial-by-trial basis, ORN gain was correlated with the c.d.f slope (r2 = 0.7) (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The gain changed within ~130 ms following the change in stimulus variance.
source: In these experiments, the gain changed within ~130 ms following the change in stimulus variance (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Changing the stimulus mean alone changed gain in LFP.
source: Changing the stimulus mean alone changed gain in LFP (Figure 5a–b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: Gain at the spiking machinery was largely invariant to the ten-fold change in the mean stimulus.
source: However, gain at the spiking machinery was largely invariant to the ten-fold change in the mean stimulus (p=0.41, Spearman rank correlation), with a 1 mV change in LFP leading to a ~ 10 Hz change in the firing rate, consistent with earlier studies (Nagel and Wilson, 2011) (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5c-d, and citation to prior work.

claim: Transduction gain, like ORN gain, scaled with the Weber-Fechner Law, for a variety of odor-receptor combinations.
source: Transduction gain, like ORN gain, scaled with the Weber-Fechner Law, for a variety of odor-receptor combinations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-d) consistent with previous studies (Cafaro, 2016; Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-d and citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptation to the stimulus variance changed gain both at transduction and at spiking.
source: In contrast, adaptation to the stimulus variance changed gain both at transduction and at spiking (Figure 5e–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e-h.

claim: Both gains changed by a factor of ~1.3 from the high to the low variance epoch.
source: Both gains changed by a factor of ~1.3 from the high to the low variance epoch (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test), contributing roughly equally to variance gain control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5e-h.

claim: While increasing light levels elicited increasing firing rates, ORN and transduction gain did not vary with the intensity of supplemental light.
source: While increasing light levels elicited increasing firing rates (Figure 6b inset), ORN and transduction gain did not vary with the intensity of supplemental light (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Constitutive spiking activity does not feed back onto LFP adaptation, or overall ORN gain.
source: This suggests that constitutive spiking activity does not feed back onto LFP adaptation, or overall ORN gain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in gain with supplemental light.

claim: While ethyl acetate backgrounds of increasing intensity increased ORN firing rate, they failed to change gain in the spiking machinery.
source: While ethyl acetate backgrounds of increasing intensity increased ORN firing rate (Figure 6d inset), they failed to change gain in the spiking machinery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: Adaptation at transduction does not affect gain of the spiking machinery.
source: This suggests that adaptation at transduction does not affect gain of the spiking machinery, consistent with our result that increasing odor backgrounds decreased gain at transduction, but not spiking (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6c-d and Figure 5a-d.

claim: Weber-Fechner scaling in ORN gain control to stimulus mean is insulated from activity of the spiking machinery.
source: Thus, Weber-Fechner scaling in ORN gain control to stimulus mean is insulated from activity of the spiking machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing independent gain control at transduction and spiking.

claim: ORN input-output curves were steeper when the variance of the light stimulation was smaller.
source: ORN input-output curves were steeper when the variance of the light stimulation was smaller (Figure 6e–f), similar to the curves observed with odor stimulation (cf. Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: Gain changed by a factor of ~1.5 when the standard deviation of the light stimulus changed by a factor of ~3.
source: We observed that gain changed by a factor of ~1.5 when the standard deviation of the light stimulus changed by a factor of ~3, consistent with variance gain control occurring partly in the spiking machinery (Figure 5e–h), though Chrimson channels might exhibit their own nonlinear activation properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e-f and inference about the mechanism.

claim: For stimuli on low backgrounds, LFP cross-correlation functions peaked earlier, while for stimuli on larger backgrounds, LFP cross-correlation functions peaked later.
source: For stimuli on low backgrounds, LFP cross-correlation functions peaked earlier, while for stimuli on larger backgrounds, LFP cross-correlation functions peaked later (Figure 7a), consistent with previous results (Cao et al., 2016; Kaissling et al., 1987; Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a and citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-correlation functions from the stimulus to the firing rate were similar between stimuli on low and high backgrounds.
source: Surprisingly, cross-correlation functions from the stimulus to the firing rate were similar between stimuli on low and high backgrounds (Figure 7b), consistent with (Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and citation to prior work.

claim: LFP response lags increased with increasing odorant concentration.
source: We defined the LFP and firing rate lags relative to the stimulus by the location of the peak of the cross-correlation function, and found that while LFP response lags increased with increasing odorant concentration (p<10−2, Spearman test), firing rate lags remained relatively invariant with odorant concentration (p>0.1, Spearman test) (Figure 7d–g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7d-g.

claim: Firing rate lags remained relatively invariant with odorant concentration.
source: We defined the LFP and firing rate lags relative to the stimulus by the location of the peak of the cross-correlation function, and found that while LFP response lags increased with increasing odorant concentration (p<10−2, Spearman test), firing rate lags remained relatively invariant with odorant concentration (p>0.1, Spearman test) (Figure 7d–g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7d-g.

claim: Firing lags decreased with increasing light power concentration.
source: Firing lags decreased with increasing light power concentration (p<10−4, Spearman test), suggesting that the ORN spiking machinery can speed up with increasing mean input currents (Figure 7h), as would accompany increasing odor backgrounds (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7h, and citation to prior work.

claim: A three-fold change in the stimulus variance did not significantly change kinetics either at LFP or firing rate.
source: We found that a three-fold change in the stimulus variance, despite leading to changes in LFP and firing gains (Figures 4–5), did not significantly change kinetics either at LFP or firing rate (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), consistent with our earlier results suggesting that mean and variance gain control have distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and inference about distinct mechanisms.

claim: Response lags of the model with respect to the stimulus increased with the mean stimulus.
source: In addition, response lags of this model with respect to the stimulus increased with the mean stimulus (Figure 8e), similar to the slowdown observed in the LFP responses (cf. Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The model can reproduce LFP responses to naturalistic, intermittent signals.
source: Finally, this model can also reproduce LFP responses to naturalistic, intermittent signals, approximating well the time trace (Figure 8f,h) and the dependence on previous whiffs (Figure 8g, compare to Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 8f-h.

claim: LFP signals were generated upstream of the spiking machinery.
source: Previous results have shown that: LFP responses are unaffected by the addition of TTX, which eliminates neural spiking, suggesting that LFP signals were generated upstream of the spiking machinery; and that LFP signals are unaffected when the neuron's partner cell in the sensillum is genetically ablated, when that partner does not sense the odorant, suggesting that LFP signals are generated by the neuron of interest (Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work characterizing LFP signals.

claim: The LFP serves as an imperfect but useful proxy for transduction activity in ORNs.
source: Though the LFP could reflect activity of nearby sensilla, it serves as an imperfect but useful proxy for transduction activity in ORNs (Johnston et al., 1995; Kaissling, 1986; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing LFP signals.

claim: Durations of whiffs and blanks were broadly distributed, with a power law of exponent −3/2 to match natural intermittent statistics of odor plumes.
source: Durations of whiffs and blanks were broadly distributed, with a power law of exponent −3/2 to match natural intermittent statistics of odor plumes (Celani et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental stimulus design and citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: PNs are most sensitive to ORN firing rates of below ~50 Hz.
source: The ORNs' postsynaptic partners, the projection neurons (PNs)(Olsen et al., 2010), are most sensitive to ORN firing rates of below ~50 Hz (Jeanne and Wilson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing PN sensitivity.

claim: Gain scaling at ORNs could act to maintain ORN firing rates in the range that PNs are most sensitive to for a wide range of concentrations, avoiding saturation of the ORN-PN synapse.
source: Thus, gain scaling at ORNs could act to maintain ORN firing rates in the range that PNs are most sensitive to for a wide range of concentrations, avoiding saturation of the ORN-PN synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on ORN gain control and cited work on PN sensitivity.

claim: Photoreceptors do not exhibit variance gain control.
source: Photoreceptors do not exhibit variance gain control, and variance adaptation arises only in the subsequent processing in bipolar cells and ganglion cells (Baccus and Meister, 2002; Kim and Rieke, 2001; Rieke, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on visual system adaptation.

claim: Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model neurons exhibit variance gain control.
source: Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model neurons exhibit variance gain control (Hong et al., 2008; Lundstrom et al., 2008; Yu and Lee, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Simpler neuron models, like the FitzHugh-Nagamo model and the linear integrate-and-fire (LIF) model also exhibit variance-dependent gain control.
source: Simpler neuron models, like the FitzHugh-Nagamo model (Hong et al., 2007), and the linear integrate-and-fire (LIF) model (Yu and Lee, 2003) also exhibit variance-dependent gain control.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Non-spiking bipolar neurons show variance gain control.
source: In the visual system, non-spiking bipolar neurons show variance gain control (Baccus and Meister, 2002; Rieke, 2001) so mechanisms for variance gain control in the absence of spike generation might be similar between these systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on visual system adaptation and inference about potential similarities.

claim: Responses to brief pulses of odorant reduced gain on timescales as brief as 500 ms.
source: Other studies using paired pulse protocols (Cao et al., 2016) found that responses to brief pulses of odorant reduced gain on timescales as brief as 500 ms, which is close to the timescale of the neural response to odors (Kim et al., 2011; Martelli et al., 2013; Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on ORN adaptation timescales.

claim: Dynamic inhibition in the antennal lobe would permit PNs to remain sensitive to rapid changes in ORN firing rate.
source: Dynamic inhibition in the antennal lobe (Nagel et al., 2015; Raccuglia et al., 2016) would permit PNs to remain sensitive to these rapid changes in ORN firing rate, ensuring propagation of information about odor encounters to the brain.
evidence: This is inferred from citations to prior work on antennal lobe processing and the experimental results on ORN gain control.

claim: Flies fly fast (~30 cm/s).
source: For flies, this task is challenging since they fly fast (~30 cm/s) (Tammero and Dickinson, 2002) and odor filaments are narrow (Murlis et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on fly flight behavior.

claim: Flies experience plume contact and plume loss in quick succession (10–250 ms).
source: Even for relatively broad and static odor plumes, flies are within odor plumes so briefly that they experience plume contact and plume loss in quick succession (10–250 ms) (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on fly odor plume navigation.

claim: Olfactory search behavior consists of rapid flight surges on encountering odor plumes, and stereotyped crosswind casts on losing odor plumes.
source: Olfactory search behavior in this setting consists of rapid flight surges on encountering odor plumes, and stereotyped crosswind casts on losing odor plumes (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on fly odor plume navigation.

claim: Navigation based on odor intensities alone may not be possible at length scales longer than 10 cm.
source: Navigation based on odor intensities alone may not be possible, as odor intensities are not informative about the direction to the odor source at length scales longer than 10 cm (Murlis et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on odor plume structure.

claim: Kinetics of transduction slowed during adaptation.
source: Previous studies have shown that kinetics of transduction slowed during adaptation (Cao et al., 2016; Nagel and Wilson, 2011), but kinetics of firing rate did not (Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on ORN adaptation kinetics.

claim: The spiking machinery speeds the kinetics back up.
source: Here we reproduced both findings and resolved this apparent contradiction. We discovered that the spiking machinery speeds the kinetics back up.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing complementary kinetic changes at transduction and spiking.

claim: The timing of short odorant encounters is preserved in neural encoding, regardless of intensity.
source: These complementary kinetic mechanisms mean that the timing of short odorant encounters is preserved in neural encoding, regardless of intensity.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing invariant firing rate kinetics despite changes in stimulus intensity.

claim: Such an encoding scheme could aid insects in navigating odor plumes to their source.
source: Such an encoding scheme could aid insects in navigating odor plumes to their source.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and knowledge of insect navigation behavior.

claim: Olfactory receptors (ORs) adapt and have co-evolved with flight.
source: Interestingly, olfactory adaptation is linked to flight in insects. Olfactory receptors (ORs) adapt and have co-evolved with flight (Edwards, 1997; Getahun et al., 2013; Jones et al., 2005), and occur only in flying insects (Missbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on olfactory receptor evolution.

claim: ORs occur only in flying insects.
source: Olfactory receptors (ORs) adapt and have co-evolved with flight (Edwards, 1997; Getahun et al., 2013; Jones et al., 2005), and occur only in flying insects (Missbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on olfactory receptor evolution.

claim: The more ancient ionotropic receptors do not appear to adapt to prolonged odor stimuli.
source: In contrast, the more ancient ionotropic receptors (Missbach et al., 2014), found in all insects, do not appear to adapt to prolonged odor stimuli (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on ionotropic receptor properties.

claim: The statistics of odor signals close to surfaces, and in the air, where flying insects encounter them, may be very different.
source: While ORs play an important role in larval olfactory navigation (Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Mathew et al., 2013; Schulze et al., 2015; Gepner et al., 2015), the statistics of odor signals close to surfaces, and in the air, where flying insects encounter them, may be very different (Murlis et al., 1992) (Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on odor plume structure and speculation about differences.

claim: Receptors capable of fast adaptation may allow flying insects to detect brief whiffs of airborne odors.
source: Receptors capable of fast adaptation may allow flying insects to detect brief whiffs of airborne odors.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and knowledge of insect flight and olfaction.

claim: The ab3 sensillum was identified by its size and location on the antenna, test pulses of 2-heptanone, spike shapes, and spontaneous firing.
source: The ab3 sensillum was identified by (1) its size and location on the antenna (2) test pulses of 2-heptanone, to which the B neuron is very sensitive, (3) spike shapes (A spikes are larger than B spikes) and (4) spontaneous firing (ab3B fires at a higher rate than ab3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used to identify sensilla.

claim: All sensilla recorded from in this study contained two neurons.
source: All sensilla recorded from in this study contained two neurons (de Bruyne et al., 1999; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing sensillum anatomy.

claim: Spike amplitude and spike shape changed with strong odor or light drive, due to a phenomenon called 'pinching'.
source: However, spike amplitude and spike shape changed in our experiments with strong odor or light drive, due to a phenomenon called 'pinching' (Olsson et al., 2006), and due to small movements of the recording electrode relative to the sensillum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and observation during experiments.

claim: The spike-sorting package performed with 99.5% accuracy compared to manually sorted data on a test dataset.
source: This spike-sorting package performed with 99.5% accuracy compared to manually sorted data on a test dataset.
evidence: This is supported by validation of the spike-sorting method.

claim: The PID was calibrated by depleting known volumes of pure odorants, and the response of the PID was found to be approximately linear with odorant flux.
source: The PID was calibrated by depleting known volumes of pure odorants, and the response of the PID was found to be approximately linear with odorant flux (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the calibration method and results.

claim: Due to gradual changes in the sensitivity of the PID detector, odor intensity measurements are not comparable across experiments.
source: However, due to gradual changes in the sensitivity of the PID detector, odor intensity measurements are not comparable across experiments.
evidence: This is a limitation noted based on observations during experiments.

claim: Using pure odorant and gas phase dilution permitted excellent reproducibility of the odor stimulus.
source: Using pure odorant and gas phase dilution permitted excellent reproducibility of the odor stimulus.
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental method.

claim: Linear filters can be reliably estimated even in the presence of a output nonlinearity for white Gaussian inputs.
source: Linear filters can be reliably estimated even in the presence of a output nonlinearity for white Gaussian inputs (Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior methodological work.

claim: Linear filters extracted from naturalistic stimuli are not unbiased estimates of the true filter, since the stimulus is not Gaussian.
source: Linear filters extracted from naturalistic stimuli (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) are not unbiased estimates of the true filter, since the stimulus is not Gaussian.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on established knowledge of filter estimation.

claim: Linear filters computed by least squares fitting are the filters that best predict R given S, in the least-squares sense.
source: Nonetheless, linear filters computed by least squares fitting are the filters that best predict R given S, in the least-squares sense.
evidence: This is a methodological statement based on established knowledge of least-squares fitting.

claim: A simple coding strategy maximizes a neuron's information capacity by matching its input-output curve to the cumulative distribution function (c.d.f) of the stimulus.
source: A simple coding strategy maximizes a neuron's information capacity by matching its input-output curve to the cumulative distribution function (c.d.f) of the stimulus (Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior theoretical work on efficient coding.

claim: As the input variance changed by a factor of 2.5, the gain in the neuron only changed by a factor of 1.7, not as much as would be required for optimal information encoding.
source: However, as the input variance changed by a factor of 2.5, the gain in the neuron only changed by a factor of 1.7, not as much as would be required for optimal information encoding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to theoretical predictions.

claim: Decreasing extracellular calcium levels, or internal free calcium, breaks Weber-Fechner gain scaling at transduction.
source: Decreasing extracellular calcium levels, or internal free calcium, breaks Weber-Fechner gain scaling at transduction (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on calcium's role in adaptation.

claim: Autoregulation of Orco via cAMP signaling has been implicated in adaptation of ORNs.
source: Other mechanisms have also been implicated in adaptation of ORNs, like autoregulation of Orco via cAMP signaling (Getahun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on ORN adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Some adaptation mechanisms act on fast timescales of several hundred milliseconds.
source: While slower adaptive processes also exist, our data on responses to naturalistic stimuli (Figures 1 and 2), and data from paired-pulse experiments (Cao et al., 2016), suggest that some adaptation mechanisms act on fast timescales of several hundred milliseconds.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: Many models that decrease gain with increasing mean stimulus also speed up response kinetics.
source: Many models that decrease gain with increasing mean stimulus also speed up response kinetics (Clark et al., 2013; De Palo et al., 2012; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Schulze et al., 2015; Seung, 2003), describing well the phenomenology of other sensory systems where gain and response speed trade off (Baylor and Hodgkin, 1974; Dunn et al., 2007; Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Payne and Howard, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling and experimental work.

claim: In olfactory systems, transduction kinetics slow down with increasing stimulus background, both in insect ORNs and in vertebrate ORNs.
source: However, in olfactory systems, transduction kinetics slow down with increasing stimulus background, both in insect ORNs (Figure 7, (Cao et al., 2016; Nagel and Wilson, 2011)) and in vertebrate ORNs (Reisert and Matthews, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: The model architecture is similar to that of the bacterial chemotaxis system and ensures that for increasing values of S, the changes in ε compensate for changes in free energy due to ligand binding.
source: The architecture of this feedback is similar to that of the bacterial chemotaxis system and ensures that for increasing values of S, the changes in ε compensate for changes in free energy due to ligand binding (Barkai and Leibler, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on bacterial chemotaxis and inference about the model properties.

claim: This kinetic property emerges because the switching rates are decreasing functions of the free energy difference ε and the requirement of Weber-Fechner scaling causes the adapted value of ε to scale with the logarithm of the mean signal intensity.
source: It is interesting to note that this kinetic property emerges because (1) the switching rates are decreasing functions of the free energy difference ε and (2) the requirement of Weber-Fechner scaling, which causes the adapted value of ε to scale with the logarithm of the mean signal intensity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model properties based on its mathematical structure.
